meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Most of the evil in this world is done by people with good intentions'?
meta.ogDescription: Not C.S. Lewis and not T.S. Eliot. It is an anonymous adage traced to a 1914 trade journal, with Lewis contributing only a thematic parallel.

answer.label: Not C.S. Lewis — an anonymous adage
answer.authorName: C.S. Lewis (credited, but did not write it)
answer.sourceLine: C.S. Lewis never wrote this sentence — and neither did T.S. Eliot, to whom it is pinned even more often. Quote Investigator traces the saying to an anonymous 1914 trade-journal item and finds no single author. Lewis’s only connection is a thematic parallel in his 1949 essay “The Humanitarian Theory of Punishment”; the closest near-exact wording actually belongs to Ayn Rand’s 1945 private journal.

source.heading: What the record shows

docMeta.dd: C.S. Lewis — and, even more often, T.S. Eliot
An anonymous adage with no established author

source.excerpt: “Most of the evil in this world is done by people with good intentions.”
trail: Quote Investigator locates the earliest match in the November 1914 issue of a dairy trade journal, The Creamery and Milk Plant Monthly: “the greatest harm in the world has been done by people with good intentions.”

The exact modern wording is most often pinned on T.S. Eliot — Goodreads files it under his name with more than a thousand likes and no cited work — yet QI found “no evidence that T. S. Eliot wrote or spoke the statement.”

C.S. Lewis’s link is thematic only: his 1949 essay “The Humanitarian Theory of Punishment” warns that “a tyranny sincerely exercised for the good of its victims may be the most oppressive” — a related idea, not this sentence.
The closest near-exact phrasing belongs to Ayn Rand’s 1945 journal — “most of the evil in this world is done by and through ‘good’ intentions” — per QI.
source.excerptNote: The earliest documented near-match, located by Quote Investigator in the November 1914 issue of the dairy trade journal The Creamery and Milk Plant Monthly, read: “the greatest harm in the world has been done by people with good intentions. The bad ones seldom have power enough to do great harm.”
source.rightsNote: The exact modern wording cannot be tied to any single authored work. The earliest documented near-match is an anonymous 1914 trade-journal item (public-domain by age), but that is a different phrasing, and the popular sentence itself has no identifiable author or first publication — so no copyright status can be asserted for it.

author.name: C.S. Lewis
author.heading: About the credited author
author.metaLine: 1898–1963 · British writer, scholar and Christian apologist
author.bio: Clive Staples Lewis was an Oxford and Cambridge literary scholar and one of the twentieth century’s most-quoted Christian writers, author of The Chronicles of Narnia, Mere Christianity and The Screwtape Letters. His aphoristic style and moral seriousness make him a magnet for online misattribution, and quotable lines — including this one — are routinely pinned on him with no source. He did write closely related ideas about the dangers of well-meaning power, but not this exact sentence.

misattribution.heading: Often misattributed
misattribution.intro: This is a classic free-floating adage: a broadly true observation that many writers reached independently, which then gets crystallised into one memorable sentence and pinned on whichever famous name feels right. It travels under at least two big names.

items.why: This is the dominant misattribution online. Goodreads files the exact sentence under Eliot with over a thousand likes and no cited work, but Quote Investigator found “no evidence that T. S. Eliot wrote or spoke the statement.”

Lewis is credited because he wrote closely related lines about well-meaning power — e.g. his 1949 essay “The Humanitarian Theory of Punishment” — but QI classes his connection as a thematic match, not the saying itself. Wikiquote’s sourced Lewis page does not list this sentence among his words at all.
A 1949 conversation recorded by June Bingham has Niebuhr saying “most of the evil in this world does not come from evil people” — a different formulation of the same idea, per QI.

misattribution.truthLine: Per Quote Investigator, this is an anonymous adage with no established author; the earliest known match is an unsigned 1914 trade-journal item, and neither Eliot nor Lewis wrote the popular sentence.

context.heading: Why the name keeps changing
lead: The thought — that sincere, self-satisfied virtue does more damage than open villainy — is old and widely shared, which is exactly why it is so hard to pin down. Quote Investigator documents independent versions from an anonymous dairy trade journal (1914), the political writer Isabel Paterson (1943), Ayn Rand’s journals (1945), the theologians Reinhold Niebuhr (1949) and Krister Stendahl, and, as a thematic cousin, C.S. Lewis (1949).

When a sentiment is this diffuse, memes tend to freeze it into one crisp line and hand it to a marquee name. Eliot and Lewis both fit the ‘wise, literary, morally serious’ profile, so the sentence drifts to them — even though the earliest documented wording came from an unsigned note about, of all things, the creamery business.
context.pull: The earliest known version came from an anonymous 1914 note in a dairy trade journal — not from Eliot or Lewis.
